meta.title: Who really said "Success consists of going from failure to failure without loss of enthusiasm"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Not Churchill. This popular line appears nowhere in his works; it circulated anonymously from at least 1953 before being pinned on him in the 1980s.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Success consists of going from failure to failure without loss of enthusiasm'?
meta.ogDescription: Churchill never said it. The saying is anonymous, documented from 1953, and later misattributed to Churchill and Lincoln alike.

answer.label: Not Winston Churchill — an anonymous saying he never spoke or wrote
answer.authorDates: Earliest documented anonymously in 1953; pinned on Churchill by the 1980s
answer.sourceLine: This line appears nowhere in Churchill’s speeches, books, letters, or diaries. Quote Investigator traces the earliest close match to a 1953 public-speaking manual where it is given anonymously — “Success has been defined as the ability to go from failure to failure…” — and Churchill’s own editor Richard Langworth files it under “false attributions.”

source.heading: The paper trail

docMeta.dd: How to Say a Few Words (1953), p. 109

source.excerpt: Success consists of going from failure to failure without loss of enthusiasm.
trail: The earliest close match is anonymous, in David Guy Powers’ 1953 How to Say a Few Words, per Quote Investigator.
By the 1980s the once-anonymous saying was being credited to Churchill — and, nearly as often, to Abraham Lincoln — with no source in either man’s works, again per Quote Investigator.
Churchill’s estate editor Richard Langworth lists it among the lines the International Churchill Society flags as falsely attributed.
source.excerptNote: Popular wording. The earliest documented form is different and anonymous: “Success has been defined as the ability to go from failure to failure…” (1953).
source.rightsNote: The exact popular wording has no identifiable author — it circulated anonymously and cannot be tied to a specific authored, dated work, so no copyright status can be asserted. The earliest documented form appears anonymously in a 1953 book; whoever coined the maxim is unknown.

author.name: Winston Churchill
author.heading: About Winston Churchill
author.metaLine: 1874–1965 · British prime minister, statesman & Nobel laureate in Literature
author.bio: Sir Winston Churchill led Britain through the Second World War and won the 1953 Nobel Prize in Literature for his historical writing and oratory. Precisely because he was such a prolific and quotable writer, he has become one of the internet’s great “quote magnets” — anonymous aphorisms are routinely pinned on him. His own estate’s editor, Richard Langworth, keeps a running catalogue of the many sayings falsely put in his mouth, and this is one of them.

cite.sourceCitation: Earliest documented in David Guy Powers, How to Say a Few Words (New York: Dodd, Mead, 1953), 109, where the saying is presented anonymously; investigated in Garson O’Toole, “Success Is Going from Failure to Failure Without Losing Your Enthusiasm,” Quote Investigator, June 28, 2014.
cite.pageCitation: Quotle.info. “Who really said ‘Success consists of going from failure to failure without loss of enthusiasm’?” Last verified 14 Jul 2026.

copyAttribution: Anonymous saying, misattributed to Winston Churchill — earliest documented anonymously in 1953 (per Quote Investigator).

misattribution.heading: Often misattributed
misattribution.intro: This is one of the most-shared “Churchill” lines that Churchill never said. The wording circulated anonymously for decades before famous names were attached.

items.why: No speech, book, letter, or diary by Churchill contains this line. His estate’s editor Richard Langworth places it in the “Red Herrings: False Attributions” section of Churchill By Himself, and the International Churchill Society lists it among quotes he never said.
An almost equal number of online sources credit Lincoln, but Quote Investigator found no support in the Lincoln archives either.

misattribution.truthLine: The earliest documented version is anonymous: a 1953 public-speaking manual, How to Say a Few Words, phrased it “Success has been defined as the ability to go from failure to failure…” with no author named — per Quote Investigator.

context.heading: Why this gets pinned on Churchill
lead: The sentiment — that resilience matters more than an unbroken record of wins — is exactly the kind of pithy, forceful line that sounds Churchillian, which is precisely why it drifted to him. Sayings feel more authoritative when attached to a famous orator, so an anonymous 1950s maxim about public speaking gradually acquired a marquee name.
By the 1980s the once-anonymous line was being confidently credited to Churchill (and, almost as often, to Abraham Lincoln), even though it survives in neither man’s documented words.
context.pull: An anonymous maxim in search of a famous mouth — and Churchill’s was the one it found.
